gabarito.reason:
Helper.getFingerprint(Context) (Helper.java:3297-3317) uses SHA1 to hash the app's own APK signing certificate (PackageManager GET_SIGNATURES, signatures[0]) and returns it as uppercase hex. This is not a security check. It only tells the app which channel built the copy that is running. hasValidFingerprint() and isSignedByFDroid() compare the result for an exact match against three hard-coded SHA-1 hex constants in res/values/strings.xml:3047-3049 (fingerprint, fingerprint_fdroid, fingerprint_amazon). The result decides which channel the app reports to (GitHub/Play, F-Droid or Amazon), which crash reporting, update checks and donate/pro links apply, and some UI paths in Log, FragmentSetup, FragmentMessages, ActivityView and AdapterMessage. FragmentOptionsMisc:2722 also shows it to the user as the 'signature fingerprint'. Collision attacks on SHA-1 do not matter here. Passing the check would need a second preimage against a fixed certificate, and anyone who can repackage the APK can simply patch the check out, so a stronger hash adds no protection. The value is also a well-known identifier in SHA-1 form (it is the format F-Droid, Play and keytool list). Changing it to SHA-256 would make every stored constant fail to match unless all three were replaced with correct SHA-256 values of the real signing certificates. Those values cannot be worked out from this repository, and a wrong value would quietly misclassify official builds. So the RVSec MessageDigestSpec finding is a false positive in context. A PR brings risk and no benefit, and an issue would only take up the maintainers' time. The two-argument getFingerprint(context, hash) already lets callers ask for a stronger hash if they ever need one.

Second judge: Helper.getFingerprint hashes the installed app's signing certificate (info.signatures[0]), returning uppercase hexadecimal. This is not message signing, password hashing, or TLS certificate validation. hasValidFingerprint compares it against fixed SHA-1 resources for the official and Amazon signers; isSignedByFDroid compares a separate F-Droid pin. These results control update checks, Gmail/OAuth setup access, support UI, third-party warnings, and release classification. The fingerprint is also displayed in miscellaneous settings. SHA-256 hardening is reasonable, but changing only the algorithm would make every existing pin comparison fail. An issue explaining the coordinated migration is acceptable. NO_ACTION is also defensible: matching an already fixed certificate fingerprint requires a second-preimage attack, which known SHA-1 collision attacks do not provide, and Android verifies APK signatures separately. The report alone does not establish an exploitable vulnerability. No stored account data or network protocol was found to depend on this helper's digest.
must_change: For a hardening PR, migrate signing-certificate identification to SHA-256 or an equally sound certificate comparison, updating both hasValidFingerprint and isSignedByFDroid consistently.

Replace all three SHA-1 fingerprint resources with verified values for the same signing certificates. Compute new fingerprints from the original certificate bytes, not from the old SHA-1 strings. README.md supplies the official signer's SHA-256 value; equivalent verified values are needed for Amazon and F-Droid.
Keep digest encoding and comparisons consistent, and keep the displayed fingerprint understandable if its algorithm changes. Verify official, Amazon, F-Droid, and unrelated signer outcomes.
must_not_break: Correct detection of the official GitHub/Play build via hasValidFingerprint() against the stored SHA-1 constant R.string.fingerprint (17BA15C1...)
Detection of the Amazon build via R.string.fingerprint_amazon and the F-Droid build via isSignedByFDroid()/R.string.fingerprint_fdroid

Behaviour that depends on hasValidFingerprint (crash reporting in Log.java, update checks in ActivityView, pro/donate/support links in FragmentSetup/FragmentMessages/AdapterMessage/FragmentOptionsMisc, installer reporting in Helper/DebugHelper)
Format of the signature fingerprint shown in FragmentOptionsMisc (uppercase hex SHA-1, matching what keytool/F-Droid show)
Existing callers of the two-argument getFingerprint(context, hash) overload

Preserve the existing signer distinctions: official and Amazon certificates pass hasValidFingerprint; the separately pinned F-Droid certificate is recognized by isSignedByFDroid without automatically becoming an official signer.
Preserve update availability, Gmail/OAuth setup gating, support behavior, third-party warnings, and release classification for existing supported distributions, including existing debug exceptions.
Preserve compatibility with minSdkVersion 23. A digest migration must not unconditionally introduce signing-certificate APIs requiring a newer Android version.

Keep the installed signing certificates and Android package-signature verification unchanged; an internal fingerprint migration does not require re-signing releases or changing external OAuth registrations.

Do not change unrelated TLS certificate pins, S/MIME fingerprints, account or identity fingerprint fields, or backup formats merely because they also use the word fingerprint. They are separate from this helper.
Do not bypass signer checks, substitute guessed pins, or retain SHA-1 as an alternative acceptance path while claiming to eliminate reliance on it.

It correctly says all three verified SHA-256 pins are needed and that SHA-1 values cannot be converted. It suggests SHA-1 collision weakness matters here without noting that a second preimage would be needed, which is a slightly misleading security framing.

The line references (3298, 3307, 3330, 3341) check out. The reason given for not sending a PR ('fixed by a protocol or another component') is boilerplate and vague, and it never mentions the hard-coded pins or the second-preimage point.

It correctly names the three fixed 40-character pins and what they control (release identification, notices, update checks), and explains why collisions do not apply here.
